title: Time-Out For High School Students? Say What?!
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin pushes back on the assumption that removing a disruptive student from the group is exclusively an elementary strategy, arguing there's nothing age-specific about the basic right of a group to learn without interference from a disruptive individual. He clarifies that his own recommended high school classroom management plan doesn't formally include time-out the way the elementary plan does, but argues teachers should still treat it as an available option even if it isn't official policy, provided it's announced ahead of time (ideally the first day of school) so it isn't a surprise. Drawing on his own decade of high school teaching experience, he describes using this removal only three or four times total, framing it not as a behavior-correction tool per se but as an immediate, practical way to protect the rest of the class's right to learn when disruption continues despite normal consequences. He deliberately avoids formal terminology when using it in the moment ('Sit over there and chill out awhile' rather than announcing 'time-out'), arguing the substance matters more than the label.
points: There's no legitimate age cutoff for removing a disruptive student to protect the rest of the class's ability to learn -- the principle applies at any grade level.
The formal high school plan doesn't include time-out the way the elementary plan does, but teachers should still keep it as an available, pre-announced option.
Announce the possibility of removal ahead of time, ideally the first day of school, so it's never a surprise when used.
Skip formal terminology in the moment -- a plain statement like 'sit over there and chill out awhile' works better than officially invoking 'time-out.'
quotes: There is odd consensus that you can only use time-out for elementary-age students.
There is nothing wrong with removing a student who is interfering with the rights of others to learn and enjoy school. No one is too old.

Now, it’s important to point out that the two classroom management plans we recommend here at SCM—one for elementary and lower middle school and one for upper middle and high school —are very different.
I tell my high school students that if I have to sit them out to protect learning, I’ll do it because I have no other choice. The class comes first.
I don’t call it time-out. I don’t call it anything. I just say: “Zack, you can’t keep disrupting the class. Sit over there and chill out awhile.
When an older student continues to disrupt despite the regular consequences, you don’t have to take it. You don’t have to endure gross disrespect while your class loses out on their right to learn.
